```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "htbp")
template_dir <- "../../_shared/template"
source(file.path(template_dir, "viscount_rmd_helpers.R"))
library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  lines <- gsub("//.*$", "", lines)
  clean_str <- paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
  clean_str <- gsub("/\\*.*?\\*/", "", clean_str)
  clean_str <- gsub(",(\\s*[\\]\\}])", "\\1", clean_str)
  fromJSON(clean_str, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json5_clean("ecuador_after_independence.json5")
sum_data <- fromJSON("ecuador_after_independence_summary.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
sett_data <- fromJSON("ecuador_after_independence_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
ledger_data <- read_json5_clean("ecuador_after_independence_source_ledger.json5")
```

# Abstract

Ecuador parted from Gran Colombia in May 1830 with roughly 550k inhabitants, the great majority clustered in the inter-Andean basins of the Sierra while the Pacific lowlands and Amazonian foothills remained sparsely settled. Across the 24 modern provinces covering 268.846 km² (3.180 five-arcminute cells), the harmonised national series rises from 1,27M (1.271.862) at the regional compilation of 1889 and 1,69M (1.693.447) in 1909 to 2,85M (2.847.931) in 1933 and 3,48M (3.483.113) at the inaugural modern national census of 1950 [@Censos2023Conciliacion; @Censos2011Resultados]. Over the ensuing seven decades, rapid mortality decline, coastal agricultural booms and Amazonian oil colonisation carried the republic through 5,05M in 1962, 6,52M in 1974, 8,68M in 1982, 9,70M in 1990, 12,16M in 2001 and 14,48M in 2010 to 16,94M (16.938.986) at the eighth national census in 2022 [@Censos2023Conciliacion; @Cedeno2025Dinamismo; @Andrade2026Leveraging]. The central geographical transformation of the post-independence era was the demographic inversion between highlands and coast: in 1909 the Sierra still held 63,8% of the population against 31,2% in the Costa, yet cacao, banana and rice frontiers, together with the port commerce of Guayaquil, lifted the Costa past the Sierra at the 1974 census (48,9% against 48,2%) and to 53,3% by 2022 (9,03M against 6,95M in the highlands) [@Herrera2021Urbanizacion; @Valle2016Territorios]. After the 1941-1942 Rio Protocol fixed the eastern border and Texaco-Gulf oil extraction opened in 1972, state-backed road corridors drew highland settlers into Sucumbíos and Orellana, lifting the Oriente from 181k in 1974 to 928,3k (5,5%) in 2022 [@Castro2019Poblaciones; @Celade2005Poblacion]. Meanwhile the Galápagos archipelago fell from 3,45k in 1889 to 1,35k in 1950 before ecotourism and conservation administration raised it to 28,58k in 2022. A sharp banking collapse and dollarisation in 1999-2000 triggered a major emigration wave to Spain and the United States [@Mosquera2016Respuestas; @Herrera2021Impacto], offset after 2015 by substantial Venezuelan and Andean transit immigration [@Enriquez2024Indicadores; @Ceja2022Migracion]. Reconciling 267 geocoded settlements across eight national censuses, the urban system remains strongly bipolar, led by Guayaquil (2,91M municipal and 3,55M metropolitan in 2022) and Quito (1,76M city proper and 2,80M metropolitan district), followed by Cuenca (612,6k), Santo Domingo (458,2k) and Ambato (377,4k) [@Ramirez2015Leyes; @Marquezsanchez2026Two].

# Background

## Republican Separation and Nineteenth-Century Counts (1830-1909)

When the Department of the South withdrew from Gran Colombia in 1830 to form the Republic of Ecuador, its demographic centre of gravity had scarcely shifted since late Bourbon times. Quito, Cuenca and Riobamba anchored a highland society of haciendas and indigenous communes strung along cool volcanic valleys between 2.200 m and 3.100 m above sea level, whereas the tropical plains of the Guayas basin and Manabí were thinly peopled and checked by yellow fever, malaria and seasonal flooding [@Valle2016Territorios; @Celade2005Poblacion; @Coralalmeida2024Ethnic]. Early republican headcounts were sporadic fiscal or ecclesiastical lists rather than synchronous enumerations. Gabriel García Moreno's administration organised partial parish counts between 1857 and 1861 that pointed to roughly 1,0M inhabitants, though highland parishes were far more thoroughly tallied than coastal estates or forest missions [@Censos2023Conciliacion].

Throughout the mid-nineteenth century, mortality remained high and transport fractured. Steep cordillera mule paths isolated Quito from the Pacific port of Guayaquil during the rainy winter months, while frequent earthquakes - notably the 1868 Imbabura tremor around Ibarra and Otavalo - inflicted sharp local demographic shocks in the northern Sierra. Even so, natural increase in the densely farmed Andean valleys gradually filled available hacienda lands, priming a surplus rural workforce for downward migration toward the coast once commercial export agriculture took hold [@Valle2016Territorios; @Cainurquizo2025Indigenas].

By the late 1880s, steam navigation on the Guayas River and rising European demand for fine-aroma *Arriba* cacao turned the lower alluvial valleys of Los Ríos, Guayas and El Oro into Ecuador's economic engine. The 1889 provincial compilation records 1,27M residents across the republic, with 763,9k (60,1%) in the ten Sierra provinces and 368,8k (29,0%) across the coastal belt [@Censos2011Resultados]. Guayaquil already numbered 44,5k inhabitants, overtaking Quito (40k) for the first time since independence and establishing the coastal-highland rivalry that has structured Ecuadorian politics ever since [@Marquezsanchez2026Two; @Testori2018Alternative]. By 1909, as the Guayaquil and Quito Railway linked the port to the Andean plateau and cacao exports neared their pre-war zenith, national population reached 1,69M: Pichincha stood at 230,9k, Azuay at 200k and Guayas at 200k, while Manabí doubled in two decades from 64,3k to 120k [@Censos2023Conciliacion].

## Cacao Crisis, Border Settlement and the 1950 Census (1909-1950)

The first half of the twentieth century brought severe economic shocks alongside steady public-health gains. After 1914, competition from West African plantations and the spread of witches' broom (*escoba de bruja*) and monilia pod rot ruined Ecuador's cacao estates, depressing coastal export revenues through the 1920s and the Great Depression. Yet mortality fell as municipal waterworks, vaccination campaigns and port sanitation curtailed cholera and yellow fever in Guayaquil and Esmeraldas [@Testori2018Alternative; @Andrade2026Leveraging]. In the 1933 pre-war benchmark, Ecuador reached 2,85M inhabitants, with the Costa's share edging upward to 32,8% (934,8k) while the Sierra held 56,6% (1,61M).

Simultaneously, the 1895 Liberal Revolution under Eloy Alfaro accelerated secular civil registration, abolished Indian tribute vestiges and expanded rail and coastal steamship links, shifting merchant capital from landed estates in the Sierra toward Guayaquil's export-import banking houses [@Marquezsanchez2026Two; @Moser2010Gendered]. Small-scale Panama hat (*sombrero de paja toquilla*) weaving in Azuay, Cañar and Manabí provided crucial non-farm cash income during the inter-war agricultural slump, moderating distress migration out of the southern highlands until post-war industrial competition eroded artisan exports [@Jara2015Evaluando; @Reyesjaramillo2020Proceso].

Territorial definition in the Amazonian east remained contested with Peru until the short 1941 war and the Rio Protocol of January 1942, which fixed the eastern boundary along the Andean foothills and upper Napo, Pastaza and Santiago basins, leaving Ecuador with roughly 268.846 km² of continental and insular territory [@Castro2019Poblaciones]. Eight years later, in November 1950, the newly professionalised statistical office conducted Ecuador's first modern, simultaneous national census under United Nations standards [@Censos2023Conciliacion; @Censos2011Resultados]. The harmonised 1950 series places total population at 3,48M (3.483.113), revealing a country already transformed by coastal migration: the Costa had climbed to 1,46M (42,0%), driven by Manabí (401,4k) and Guayas (582,1k), while the Sierra's share had narrowed to 53,3% (1,86M).

## Banana Boom, Agrarian Reform and Oil Colonisation (1950-1990)

Between 1948 and 1965, Ecuador became the world's leading exporter of Cavendish and Gros Michel bananas. Unlike cacao, which had been concentrated on traditional Guayas and Los Ríos estates, banana smallholdings and plantations spread rapidly into Esmeraldas, El Oro, southern Guayas and the humid piedmont around Santo Domingo de los Colorados and Quevedo [@Herrera2021Urbanizacion; @Cedeno2025Dinamismo]. Highway construction connecting Quito to Santo Domingo and Esmeraldas, together with the eradication of malaria across the coastal lowlands, unleashed massive internal migration from densely settled highland provinces such as Chimborazo, Bolívar, Cotopaxi, Loja and Azuay [@Valle2016Territorios; @Cainurquizo2025Indigenas]. At the 1962 census, total population passed 5,05M, and the Sierra fell below half of the national total for the first time (48,7% against 47,7% on the coast).

Two structural shifts accelerated redistribution in the 1960s and 1970s. First, the Agrarian Reform Laws of 1964 and 1973 abolished the *huasipungo* debt-labour system on Sierra haciendas, freeing highland Kichwa and mestizo peasants to move while encouraging mechanised livestock farming that reduced rural labour demand [@Valle2016Territorios; @Celade2005Poblacion]. Cooperative estates in Cayambe, Chimborazo and Cotopaxi fragmented into tiny *minifundio* plots unable to support growing families, pushing seasonal and permanent migrants toward Quito's construction sites and Guayaquil's informal peripheries [@Valle2016Territorios; @Cainurquizo2025Indigenas]. Second, the discovery of commercial petroleum in Lago Agrio in 1967 and the opening of the Trans-Ecuadorian Pipeline in 1972 turned the northern Oriente into a state-sponsored colonisation frontier [@Castro2019Poblaciones]. Dirt roads built by oil consortia across Napo and Sucumbíos brought thousands of landless farmers from Loja, Bolívar and Pichincha into the upper Amazon. By the 1974 census (6,52M), the Costa narrowly surpassed the Sierra (48,9% against 48,2%), and by 1982 (8,68M) coastal provinces held an outright majority of 50,7%, while the Oriente more than doubled from 181k in 1974 to 445,2k [@Castro2019Poblaciones; @Censos2011Resultados].

## Dollarisation, Emigration and Recent Censuses (1990-2026)

Demographic growth decelerated markedly after 1982 as total fertility fell from over five children per woman in the 1970s to near replacement level by the 2010s [@Censos2023Conciliacion; @Cedeno2025Dinamismo]. National totals advanced from 9,70M in 1990 to 12,16M in 2001 and 14,48M in 2010 [@Censos2011Resultados]. The severe financial crisis of 1998-2000, culminating in bank freezes and the replacement of the sucre with the US dollar in January 2000, triggered the largest emigration wave in Ecuadorian history. Between 1999 and 2005, hundreds of thousands of working-age Ecuadorians departed for Spain, the United States and Italy, reshaping household structure in Azuay, Cañar, Loja and urban Guayaquil while generating remittance inflows that reshaped local housing and labour supply [@Mosquera2016Respuestas; @Herrera2021Impacto].

After the 2008 global financial crisis slowed European demand for labour, circular and return migration brought many families back from Spain [@Mosquera2016Respuestas], even as Cuenca and southern Andean towns began attracting North American retirees and European academics [@Jara2026Gentrificacion; @Perezganan2023Experiencia]. From 2015 onwards, Ecuador shifted from net sender to regional receiver as hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan and smaller cohorts of Haitian migrants entered across the northern border at Rumichaca, settling in Quito, Guayaquil, Cuenca and intermediate highland towns such as Riobamba [@Candelejo2019Migracion; @Enriquez2024Indicadores; @Ceja2022Migracion]. The eighth national census in November 2022 enumerated 16.938.986 residents, confirming slower natural growth, rapid population ageing in the southern Sierra and continued coastal concentration [@Censos2023Conciliacion; @Reyesjaramillo2020Proceso; @Sangurimapacheco2026Impacto].

# Methodology

## Provincial Partition and Historical Boundary Harmonisation

To sustain comparability across nearly two centuries of administrative reorganisation, this chapter partitions Ecuador into its 24 contemporary provinces across a 3.180-cell five-arcminute spatial domain totalling 268.846 km² (or 272.872,4 km² in vector polygon area). Ecuador's provincial map expanded repeatedly after 1830 as frontier and coastal territories gained autonomy: Zamora Chinchipe and Morona Santiago were separated in 1953, Napo and Pastaza were split in 1959, Galápagos attained provincial status in 1973, Sucumbíos was carved out of Napo in 1989, Orellana followed from Napo in 1998, and Santa Elena and Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas were detached from Guayas and Pichincha respectively in November 2007 [@Censos2011Resultados; @Cedeno2025Dinamismo].

Provincial time series across all 11 benchmarks (1889, 1909, 1933, 1950, 1962, 1974, 1982, 1990, 2001, 2010 and 2022) are harmonised through a two-stage historical GIS workflow. Eight period snapshot regimes (1870, 1890, 1920, 1950, 1970, 2000, 2010 and 2025) capture contemporaneous administrative polygons from historical boundary compilations, preserving historical territorial extents before modern splits [@Andrade2026Leveraging]. Sub-administrative enumerations from INEC's 1950-2022 demographic reconciliation, 1.040 parish-level divisions and nineteenth-century *empadronamientos* are then projected onto the fixed 24-province reporting geometry using area-and-settlement-weighted pycnophylactic disaggregation so that macro-regional shares can be tracked consistently from 1889 to 2022 [@Censos2023Conciliacion; @Andrade2026Leveraging]. For analytical clarity, the 24 provinces are grouped into four standard geographical macro-regions: the Sierra (ten Andean provinces), the Costa (seven lowland and western piedmont provinces, including Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas), the Oriente (six Amazonian provinces) and the insular Galápagos province.

## Settlement Gazetteer and Metropolitan Reconciliation

Urban and cantonal population series were compiled across four exhaustive ingestion waves into a 267-entry geocoded gazetteer containing 1.487 settlement-year observations spanning 1857 to 2025 (an average of 5,57 observations per centre). Wave 1 extracted 211 cantonal and parish records from official INEC census tables covering 1950 to 2022 and post-2022 revisions [@Censos2011Resultados; @Censos2023Conciliacion]. Wave 2 added 37 entries through georeference repair and explicit separation of metropolitan aggregates for Guayaquil and Quito [@Ramirez2015Leyes; @Marquezsanchez2026Two]. Wave 3 backfilled 16 longitudinal nineteenth- and early twentieth-century city series from historical census tables for Quito, Guayaquil, Cuenca, Ambato, Riobamba, Loja, Ibarra, Latacunga and Portoviejo, and Wave 4 filled three residual sub-regional gaps across Amazonian and coastal cantons.

Crucially, municipal limits and metropolitan footprints are kept distinct to prevent double counting [@Herrera2021Urbanizacion; @Jara2015Evaluando]. In Quito, the *Distrito Metropolitano de Quito* (DMQ) encompasses rural and suburban valleys such as Calderón, Conocoto, Cumbayá, Tumbaco, Amaguaña and Yaruquí alongside the dense urban core; both the urban seat (Quito city proper) and the consolidated metropolitan aggregate are retained with explicit scope tags, while suburban parishes outside the urban core are tracked individually [@Salgado2024Rescue; @V2003Fernando]. Similarly, Guayaquil is tracked both as city proper and as a metropolitan complex linking Durán, Samborondón and Daule across the Guayas estuary [@Testori2018Alternative; @Moser2021Mothers; @Moser2010Gendered]. Nine candidate names were excluded from the active 267-entry register: six unlocated historical toponyms lacking unique parish coordinates and three duplicate variants merged into canonical cantons (*Atuntaqui* into *Antonio Ante* at 0,41 km, plus variant entries for *Bolívar* and *Olmedo*).

## Provincial Covariates and Demographic Rates

Provincial growth rates between benchmark $t_1$ and $t_2$ are computed as annualised exponential rates:

$$r = \frac{\ln(P_{t_2} / P_{t_1})}{t_2 - t_1}$$

which allows direct comparison across unequal inter-censal intervals (12 years between 1950 and 1962, 12 between 1962 and 1974, 8 between 1974 and 1982, 8 between 1982 and 1990, 11 between 1990 and 2001, 9 between 2001 and 2010 and 12 between 2010 and 2022) [@Cedeno2025Dinamismo]. Urban rank-size scaling is evaluated by ordinary least-squares regression in log-log space:

$$\ln P_i = \ln P_1 - \alpha \ln R_i$$

across all 267 settlements by peak recorded population, following the power-law diagnostics established for Ecuadorian cities [@Ramirez2015Leyes]. Biophysical covariates conditioning spatial allocation include Andean topographic relief above 3.500 m, coastal mangrove and alluvial floodplains, and fluvial access along the Guayas, Esmeraldas and upper Amazon river networks [@Coralalmeida2024Ethnic; @Andrade2026Leveraging]. Where provincial population densities are reported, figures divide the harmonised provincial count by the provincial raster area in km² so cross-province comparisons remain consistent across every benchmark.

# Testing and Validation

Arithmetic reconciliation across all 24 provinces confirms exact agreement with the national benchmark series from 1889 to 2022, with zero residual discrepancy against INEC's 1950-2022 demographic reconciliation totals [@Censos2023Conciliacion]. Table \ref{tab:validation-ecuador} summarises the harmonised macro-regional totals across all eleven benchmarks, showing the progressive shift from highland predominance to a coastal majority alongside the post-1974 expansion of the Amazonian Oriente.

```{r tab-validation, results='asis'}
benchmarks <- c("1889", "1909", "1933", "1950", "1962", "1974", "1982", "1990", "2001", "2010", "2022")
sierra_keys <- c("ecu_azuay", "ecu_bolivar", "ecu_canar", "ecu_carchi", "ecu_chimborazo", "ecu_cotopaxi", "ecu_imbabura", "ecu_loja", "ecu_pichincha", "ecu_tungurahua")
costa_keys <- c("ecu_el_oro", "ecu_esmeraldas", "ecu_guayas", "ecu_los_rios", "ecu_manabi", "ecu_santa_elena", "ecu_santo_domingo_de_los_tsachilas")
oriente_keys <- c("ecu_morona_santiago", "ecu_napo", "ecu_orellana", "ecu_pastaza", "ecu_sucumbios", "ecu_zamora_chinchipe")
gal_keys <- c("ecu_galapagos")

sum_group <- function(keys, yr) {
  sum(vapply(keys, function(k) as.numeric(mod_data$regions[[k]]$population[[yr]]), numeric(1)))
}

val_rows <- lapply(benchmarks, function(yr) {
  p_s <- sum_group(sierra_keys, yr)
  p_c <- sum_group(costa_keys, yr)
  p_o <- sum_group(oriente_keys, yr)
  p_g <- sum_group(gal_keys, yr)
  p_tot <- p_s + p_c + p_o + p_g
  data.frame(
    Year = yr,
    Sierra = viscount_fmt_pop(p_s),
    Costa = viscount_fmt_pop(p_c),
    Oriente = viscount_fmt_pop(p_o),
    Galapagos = viscount_fmt_pop(p_g),
    Total = viscount_fmt_pop(p_tot),
    Sierra_Share = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(100 * p_s / p_tot, 1L), "%"),
    Costa_Share = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(100 * p_c / p_tot, 1L), "%"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
val_df <- do.call(rbind, val_rows)
rownames(val_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  val_df,
  "Macro-regional demographic totals and regional shares across Ecuador, 1889 to 2022, harmonised to 24 provinces.",
  c("Year", "Sierra", "Costa", "Oriente", "Galápagos", "National Total", "Sierra Share", "Costa Share"),
  list(label = "tab:validation-ecuador", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

Cross-checking provincial totals against historical border regimes highlights one systematic disaggregation artefact in the raw 1974 and 1933 Oriente and newly separated provincial slices. Because the 1970 snapshot regime aggregated most of the upper Amazon under a single eastern jurisdiction and retained Santa Elena and Santo Domingo within Guayas and Pichincha prior to 2007, automated 1974 redistribution temporarily assigned 173,5k to Morona Santiago while leaving Napo (1,43k), Orellana (1,27k), Pastaza (1,10k), Sucumbíos (2,01k) and Zamora Chinchipe (1,73k) under-allocated, and similarly underestimated Santa Elena (4,42k) and Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas (6,23k) in 1974 relative to their 1962 and 1982 trajectories. Summed at the macro-regional level, however, both Oriente (181k in 1974) and Costa (3,19M in 1974) remain internally consistent and smoothly bridge the 1962 and 1982 censuses. Saturation auditing of the settlement gazetteer shows zero crowd-sourced entries (0,0% fallback share), 100% coverage of all 24 provincial masks and a marginal gain of 1,14% on the fourth verification sweep.

# Results

## National Trajectory and the Highland-to-Coast Shift (1889-2022)

Across the 133 years separating the 1889 compilation from the 2022 census, Ecuador's population multiplied more than thirteenfold, growing from 1.271.862 to 16.938.986 at an average annualised rate of 1,95% (Figure \ref{fig:traj-ecuador}) [@Censos2023Conciliacion]. Expansion was slowest in the late nineteenth century (1,43% per year between 1889 and 1909), accelerated during the inter-war mortality decline (2,17% per year from 1909 to 1933), and peaked between 1950 and 1982 at 2,85% per year as infant mortality dropped sharply while birth rates remained high [@Cedeno2025Dinamismo; @Andrade2026Leveraging]. Following the onset of fertility transition in the late 1970s and sustained emigration after 1999, national growth cooled to 1,39% per year in 1982-1990, 2,05% in 1990-2001, 1,95% in 2001-2010 and 1,31% per year between 2010 and 2022 [@Censos2011Resultados; @Mosquera2016Respuestas; @Herrera2021Impacto].

```{r fig-traj, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/ecuador_after_independence_population_trajectory.png",
  "Population trajectory across Ecuador's leading provinces from 1889 to 2022 and provincial population density in 2022.",
  "fig:traj-ecuador"
)
```

The defining regional story of modern Ecuador is the sustained demographic rebalancing from the Sierra to the Costa (Table \ref{tab:validation-ecuador}, Table \ref{tab:regions-ecuador}). In 1909, the Sierra held 1,08M people (63,8% of the republic), led by Pichincha (230,9k), Azuay (200k), Chimborazo (146,2k) and Cotopaxi (105k), while the Costa held 527,8k (31,2%). Three economic engines overturned that balance over the following seventy years. First, the cacao ports and riverine plains of Guayas and Los Ríos drew steady streams of highland seasonal labourers (*serranos*), many of whom settled permanently along the Daule, Babahoyo and Vinces tributaries [@Valle2016Territorios; @Cainurquizo2025Indigenas]. Second, the post-1948 banana boom turned El Oro (jumping from 89,3k in 1950 to 262,6k in 1974 and 714,6k in 2022), Los Ríos (150,3k to 383,4k and 898,7k) and Esmeraldas (75,4k to 203,2k and 553,9k) into major recipient provinces [@Herrera2021Urbanizacion; @Cedeno2025Dinamismo]. Third, Manabí sustained intense rural natural increase and coastal port growth around Manta and Portoviejo, expanding tenfold from 64,3k in 1889 to 627,2k in 1962 and 1,59M in 2022. By 2022, Guayas alone accounted for 4,39M inhabitants (25,9% of Ecuador), exceeding the combined population of the eight smallest Sierra provinces [@Censos2011Resultados].

Within the Sierra, growth became sharply polarised around Quito and Cuenca while agrarian provinces lagged behind [@Sangurimapacheco2026Impacto; @Reyesjaramillo2020Proceso]. Pichincha expanded sixteenfold from 187,8k in 1889 to 3,09M in 2022, reaching 353 inhabitants per km², the highest provincial density in the country ahead of Guayas (288 per km²). Tungurahua (79,6k to 563,5k, 113 per km²) and Imbabura (56,5k to 469,9k, 82 per km²) prospered on diversified commerce, textiles and flower exports [@Valle2016Territorios; @Celade2005Poblacion]. By contrast, Chimborazo (471,9k in 2022, up only 2,9% since 2010), Bolívar (199,1k), Cañar (227,6k), Carchi (172,8k) and Loja (485,4k) experienced chronic net out-migration first to Guayaquil and Quito, then to the Oriente frontier, and after 1999 to Spain and the United States [@Cainurquizo2025Indigenas; @Reyesjaramillo2020Proceso; @Mosquera2016Respuestas]. As young adults departed, southern Sierra provinces aged earlier than the national average: in Loja and Azuay, rising elderly dependency ratios became a hallmark of rural cantons between 1962 and 2022 [@Reyesjaramillo2020Proceso; @Jara2026Gentrificacion].

Along the western Andean foothills, Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas illustrates how mid-century highway corridors created entirely new demographic nodes. Linked to Quito in the 1960s and detached as an independent province in 2007, Santo Domingo grew from 239k in 1990 to 332,3k in 2001, 410,9k in 2010 and 493k in 2022 (82 inhabitants per km²), acting as the commercial hinge between highland markets and the coastal plantations of Manabí, Esmeraldas and Los Ríos [@Censos2011Resultados; @Herrera2021Urbanizacion]. Santa Elena followed a parallel trajectory along the western Guayas peninsula, rising from 169,6k in 1990 to 308,7k in 2010 and 385,7k in 2022 on fishing, salt extraction, coastal tourism and suburban spillover from Guayaquil [@Testori2018Alternative].

```{r tab-regions, results='asis'}
yr_cols <- c("1889", "1909", "1950", "1974", "1990", "2010", "2022")
reg_rows <- lapply(names(mod_data$regions), function(rk) {
  rv <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  vals <- vapply(yr_cols, function(y) viscount_fmt_pop(rv$population[[y]]), character(1))
  df_r <- data.frame(
    Province = rv$name,
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(rv$area_km2, 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  for (idx in seq_along(yr_cols)) {
    df_r[[yr_cols[idx]]] <- vals[idx]
  }
  df_r
})
reg_df <- do.call(rbind, reg_rows)

tot_vals <- vapply(yr_cols, function(y) {
  tot <- sum(vapply(mod_data$regions, function(r) as.numeric(r$population[[y]]), numeric(1)))
  viscount_fmt_pop(tot)
}, character(1))

tot_row <- data.frame(
  Province = "National Total",
  Area = viscount_fmt_number(mod_data$total_area_km2, 0L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
for (idx in seq_along(yr_cols)) {
  tot_row[[yr_cols[idx]]] <- tot_vals[idx]
}
reg_df <- rbind(reg_df, tot_row)
rownames(reg_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  reg_df,
  "Harmonised provincial population benchmarks across all 24 Ecuadorian provinces, 1889 to 2022.",
  c("Province", "Area (km²)", "1889", "1909", "1950", "1974", "1990", "2010", "2022"),
  list(label = "tab:regions-ecuador", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Oriente Oil Frontier and the Galápagos Archipelago

East of the Andes, the six Oriente provinces represent nearly 48% of Ecuador's land area (127.181 km² across Morona Santiago, Napo, Orellana, Pastaza, Sucumbíos and Zamora Chinchipe) yet long held under 5% of the population [@Castro2019Poblaciones]. Before 1972, missionary settlements, Shuar and Achuar territory in Morona Santiago, Waorani and Kichwa communities along the Napo and Curaray, and small gold-panning towns in Zamora Chinchipe maintained low densities below 2 persons per km² [@Castro2019Poblaciones; @Celade2005Poblacion]. State petroleum infrastructure changed the northern Amazon abruptly. Following the first crude exports through Balao in 1972, Nueva Loja (Lago Agrio) in Sucumbíos and Puerto Francisco de Orellana (Coca) on the Napo River became boomtown hubs for oilfield contractors and agricultural colonists clearing plots along pipeline roads. Between 1982 and 2022, Sucumbíos doubled from 94,7k to 199,0k, Orellana more than doubled from 86,7k to 182,2k, and Morona Santiago climbed from 70,2k to 192,5k, lifting the Oriente macro-region to 928,3k inhabitants (5,5% of Ecuador) in 2022 [@Castro2019Poblaciones; @Censos2011Resultados]. High indigenous fertility in Shuar, Achuar and Amazonian Kichwa parishes complemented settler inflows, keeping Amazonian growth above the national average even after oil-sector employment cooled [@Castro2019Poblaciones; @Coralalmeida2024Ethnic].

Across the Pacific, the Galápagos archipelago followed an entirely different curve. Nineteenth-century penal settlements, orchilla-moss camps and cattle estates on Floreana and San Cristóbal left an unstable population that declined from 3,45k in 1889 and 2,53k in 1909 to just 1.346 persons in 1950 [@Censos2023Conciliacion]. Following the creation of Galápagos National Park in 1959 and the inauguration of commercial air links to Baltra and San Cristóbal, nature tourism transformed the islands into a magnet for mainland coastal and highland workers. Population quadrupled from 2.468 in 1962 to 9.785 in 1990 and surged to 18.640 in 2001, prompting the 1998 Special Law for Galápagos to restrict permanent residency permits [@Censos2011Resultados]. Under strict migration controls, growth moderated to 25.124 in 2010 and 28.583 in 2022 (4,2 inhabitants per km² across 6.768 km²), concentrated in Puerto Ayora (Santa Cruz), Puerto Baquerizo Moreno (San Cristóbal) and Puerto Villamil (Isabela) [@Cedeno2025Dinamismo].

## The Bipolar Urban Hierarchy and Intermediate Cities

Unlike most Latin American republics dominated by a single primate capital, Ecuador developed a durable two-pole urban hierarchy split between commercial Guayaquil and administrative Quito (Figure \ref{fig:hier-ecuador}) [@Ramirez2015Leyes; @Marquezsanchez2026Two]. In 1857, Quito was still the larger city (36k against 22k in Guayaquil), but coastal export trade reversed their positions by 1889 (44,5k in Guayaquil against 40k in Quito). Throughout the twentieth century Guayaquil maintained its lead as Ecuador's largest city, expanding from 259k in 1950 to 510,8k in 1962, 823,2k in 1974, 1,20M in 1982, 1,99M in 2001 and 2,91M municipal (3,55M metropolitan) in 2022 [@Testori2018Alternative; @Moser2010Gendered; @Moser2021Mothers]. Much of Guayaquil's post-1960 expansion unfolded through informal tidal-flat settlements along the *Estero Salado* (*Suburbio Oeste*) and *Guasmo* before spilling across the Guayas bridge into Durán (rising from 51k in 1982 to 316,6k in 2022) and the northern suburbs of Daule (18,9k to 225,8k) and Samborondón [@Testori2018Alternative; @Moser2021Mothers; @Moser2010Gendered].

```{r fig-hier, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/ecuador_after_independence_urban_hierarchy.png",
  "Leading Ecuadorian cities and metropolitan areas by peak population and log-log rank-size scaling across 267 settlements.",
  "fig:hier-ecuador"
)
```

Quito grew more slowly until the 1970s oil boom centralised state ministries, banking and corporate headquarters in the capital. From 209,9k in 1950 and 354,7k in 1962, Quito surged to 599,8k in 1974 and 866,5k in 1982, then overflowed its narrow north-south Andean trough (*hoyas*) into the eastern valleys of Cumbayá, Tumbaco, Los Chillos (Conocoto) and the northern plateau of Calderón [@Salgado2024Rescue; @V2003Fernando]. By 2022, Quito's urban core stood at 1,76M while the broader *Distrito Metropolitano* reached 2,80M (2,86M in 2025), nearly matching Guayaquil's municipal footprint and outperforming the port in formal-sector productivity and per-capita service output [@Marquezsanchez2026Two; @Ramirez2015Leyes; @V2003Fernando].

Beneath the two metropolises, an increasingly balanced tier of intermediate regional centres absorbed rural-urban migrants after 1974 [@Herrera2021Urbanizacion; @Ramirez2015Leyes]. Across all 267 catalogued settlements, the Zipf rank-size slope sits at $\alpha = 1,06$ ($R^2 = 0,98$), close to the canonical unity benchmark (Figure \ref{fig:hier-ecuador}) [@Ramirez2015Leyes]. Cuenca solidified its rank as the third city, rising from 25k in 1889 and 99,2k in 1950 to 277,4k in 2001 and 612,6k in 2022 while undergoing heritage conservation and transnational housing pressures [@Jara2015Evaluando; @Jara2026Gentrificacion; @Perezganan2023Experiencia]. Santo Domingo de los Colorados emerged out of mid-century forest colonisation at the crossroads of the Sierra and Costa to become Ecuador's fourth urban centre (69,2k in 1982 to 334,8k urban and 458,2k cantonal in 2022). Along the coast and highlands, Ambato (377,4k in 2022), Portoviejo (336,5k), Machala (316,1k), Manta (281,1k), Riobamba (271,0k), Loja (254,5k), Esmeraldas (229,4k), Latacunga (221,0k), Ibarra (223,5k), Quevedo (219,5k), Milagro (211,8k) and Babahoyo (188,8k) now form an integrated national urban network [@Herrera2021Urbanizacion; @Candelejo2019Migracion].

## Social Composition, Internal Mobility and External Shocks

Censuses from 2001 to 2022 also illuminate the ethnic and educational geography behind provincial growth. Self-identified Indigenous Ecuadorians, concentrated in Chimborazo, Imbabura, Cotopaxi, Bolívar, Tungurahua and the Amazonian provinces, represent roughly 7% to 8% of the national total in official censuses, though highland-to-city migration has created large urban Kichwa communities in Quito and Guayaquil [@Celade2005Poblacion; @Cainurquizo2025Indigenas]. Afro-Ecuadorians remain clustered in Esmeraldas, the Chota-Mira valley of Imbabura and Carchi, and working-class districts of Guayaquil, while Montubio coastal rural communities account for over 7% of the population across Manabí, Los Ríos and Guayas [@Celade2005Poblacion; @Andrade2026Leveraging]. Health and deprivation indices compiled from census microdata reveal persistent altitude and regional gaps, with higher deprivation and maternal mortality burdens concentrated in rural Amazonian and highland indigenous parishes than in metropolitan cores [@Coralalmeida2024Ethnic; @Andrade2026Leveraging].

Recent micro-census analyses confirm that secondary and tertiary education has become the strongest predictor of internal inter-provincial migration toward Pichincha, Guayas and Azuay, draining human capital from peripheral rural cantons [@Sangurimapacheco2026Impacto; @Cedeno2025Dinamismo]. At the same time, post-2015 Venezuelan immigration (over 470k residing or transiting by 2022) and smaller Haitian flows reshaped urban labour markets and border towns from Tulcán and Ibarra to Riobamba, Quito and Guayaquil [@Enriquez2024Indicadores; @Candelejo2019Migracion; @Ceja2022Migracion], partly offsetting the demographic losses caused by renewed Ecuadorian emigration to the United States and Europe after 2021 [@Herrera2021Impacto; @Mosquera2016Respuestas].

Table \ref{tab:growth-ecuador} reports annualised inter-censal growth rates across Ecuador's four macro-regions from 1950 to 2022, computed directly from the harmonised provincial totals. National expansion peaked at 3,10% per year during the 1950-1962 banana and anti-malaria boom, remained elevated at 2,12% to 3,57% across 1962-1982 as coastal colonisation continued, and moderated steadily to 1,31% per year in 2010-2022 as fertility approached replacement level across both highlands and coast [@Cedeno2025Dinamismo; @Censos2023Conciliacion].

```{r tab-growth, results='asis'}
intervals <- list(
  c("1950", "1962"),
  c("1962", "1974"),
  c("1974", "1982"),
  c("1982", "1990"),
  c("1990", "2001"),
  c("2001", "2010"),
  c("2010", "2022")
)

rate_str <- function(keys, y1, y2) {
  p1 <- sum(vapply(keys, function(k) as.numeric(mod_data$regions[[k]]$population[[y1]]), numeric(1)))
  p2 <- sum(vapply(keys, function(k) as.numeric(mod_data$regions[[k]]$population[[y2]]), numeric(1)))
  r_pct <- 100 * log(p2 / p1) / (as.numeric(y2) - as.numeric(y1))
  paste0(viscount_fmt_number(r_pct, 2L), "%")
}

all_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)
g_rows <- lapply(intervals, function(iv) {
  y1 <- iv[1]
  y2 <- iv[2]
  data.frame(
    Interval = paste0(y1, "-", y2),
    Sierra = rate_str(sierra_keys, y1, y2),
    Costa = rate_str(costa_keys, y1, y2),
    Oriente = rate_str(oriente_keys, y1, y2),
    Galapagos = rate_str(gal_keys, y1, y2),
    National = rate_str(all_keys, y1, y2),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
g_df <- do.call(rbind, g_rows)
rownames(g_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  g_df,
  "Annualised inter-censal population growth rates by macro-region across Ecuador, 1950 to 2022.",
  c("Interval", "Sierra", "Costa", "Oriente", "Galápagos", "National"),
  list(label = "tab:growth-ecuador", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

Even as natural growth slowed, divergence between urban corridors and stagnant rural highlands sharpened after 2001 [@Sangurimapacheco2026Impacto; @Andrade2026Leveraging]. In the 2010-2022 interval, Pichincha (+19,9%), Guayas (+20,3%), Orellana (+33,6%) and Morona Santiago (+30,1%) continued absorbing migrants and sustaining youthful age structures, whereas Cañar (+1,1%), Chimborazo (+2,9%), Carchi (+5,0%) and Loja (+8,1%) expanded at less than half the national pace [@Reyesjaramillo2020Proceso; @Censos2023Conciliacion].

# Limitations

Four methodological and archival constraints bear directly on the interpretation of these figures. First, nineteenth- and early twentieth-century enumerations prior to the November 1950 census lack uniform nationwide coverage [@Censos2023Conciliacion]. The 1889, 1909 and 1933 benchmarks combine partial provincial counts, ecclesiastical parish returns and retrospective demographic back-projections; coverage of uncontacted or mobile Amazonian populations in the Oriente and scattered *Montubio* settlements on the coastal frontier carries wider uncertainty bands (roughly ±6%) than post-1950 census figures (±2,5%) [@Celade2005Poblacion; @Castro2019Poblaciones].

Second, Ecuador's recurrent creation of new provinces and cantons introduces polygon-reallocation sensitivity. As noted in the reconciliation check, the 1974 benchmark inherits boundaries from the 1970 snapshot regime in which Santa Elena, Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas, Sucumbíos and Orellana had not yet been separated from Guayas, Pichincha and Napo, producing sharp individual jumps between 1974 and 1982 even though macro-regional totals remain continuous. Similarly, the 2022 census encountered post-pandemic field delays, security disruptions in parts of Esmeraldas and Guayas, and higher non-response in gated metropolitan districts, which INEC subsequently adjusted in its 2023 demographic reconciliation [@Censos2023Conciliacion; @Andrade2026Leveraging].

Third, spatial centroid assignment places the Guayaquil metropolitan and municipal points near the Guayas-Santa Elena border zone, and treats *Distrito Metropolitano de Quito* separately from Quito's urban core; users of the settlement gazetteer must therefore avoid summing metropolitan and city-proper rows together [@Ramirez2015Leyes]. In addition, post-2010 cantonal series incorporate INEC's 2024 demographic revision through 2025, which smooths short-term migration volatility across border cantons such as Tulcán, Lago Agrio and Huaquillas [@Enriquez2024Indicadores; @Ceja2022Migracion].

Finally, the nineteenth-century and mid-century *empadronamientos* contain fewer small towns than the 2010 and 2022 censuses, so apparent growth in the number of urban nodes partly reflects improved statistical visibility rather than brand-new foundations [@Herrera2021Urbanizacion]. Readers comparing pre-1950 provincial densities with modern figures should bear in mind that early parish registers routinely undercounted dispersed coastal *recintos* and forest settlements.

# Conclusion

Between 1830 and 2026, Ecuador transformed from a fragmented Andean republic of roughly half a million people into a predominantly coastal, urbanised nation of 16,94M inhabitants. Two centuries of export cycles - *Arriba* cacao along the Guayas tributaries, Cavendish bananas across Esmeraldas, Los Ríos and El Oro, and Amazonian crude after 1972 - progressively dismantled the colonial highland monopoly and shifted the demographic centre of gravity to the Pacific lowlands [@Valle2016Territorios; @Herrera2021Urbanizacion].

By 1974 the Costa had overtaken the Sierra, and by 2022 it held 53,3% of the national population, led by the 3,55M metropolitan complex of Guayaquil [@Testori2018Alternative; @Moser2021Mothers]. Yet Quito's oil-funded administrative ascent, reaching 2,80M across its metropolitan district, preserved an enduring bipolar urban equilibrium rather than single-city primacy, supported by Cuenca, Santo Domingo, Ambato and coastal ports along a well-behaved Zipf hierarchy ($\alpha = 1,06$) [@Ramirez2015Leyes; @Marquezsanchez2026Two]. Having passed rapidly through the demographic transition while weathering the 1999-2000 dollarisation emigration shock and recent Andean immigration waves, Ecuador enters the mid-twenty-first century with slowing natural growth, an ageing southern highland interior and an urban future concentrated along the Guayaquil-Quito corridor and Pacific coast [@Mosquera2016Respuestas; @Reyesjaramillo2020Proceso].

# Appendix

Table \ref{tab:regions-extra} complements Table \ref{tab:regions-ecuador} by reporting the four remaining benchmark years (1933, 1962, 1982 and 2001) alongside 2022 provincial population density and catalogued settlement counts across all 24 provinces. Table \ref{tab:corpora-ecuador} documents the three primary national archival corpora, and Table \ref{tab:hgis-ecuador} summarises the eight historical GIS snapshot regimes underlying the provincial boundary harmonisation.

```{r tab-regions-extra, results='asis'}
extra_yrs <- c("1933", "1962", "1982", "2001")
ext_rows <- lapply(names(mod_data$regions), function(rk) {
  rv <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  ar <- as.numeric(rv$area_km2)
  p22 <- as.numeric(rv$population[["2022"]])
  n_sites <- sum(vapply(sett_data, function(s) identical(s$region_id, rk), logical(1)))
  df_r <- data.frame(
    Province = rv$name,
    Y1933 = viscount_fmt_pop(rv$population[["1933"]]),
    Y1962 = viscount_fmt_pop(rv$population[["1962"]]),
    Y1982 = viscount_fmt_pop(rv$population[["1982"]]),
    Y2001 = viscount_fmt_pop(rv$population[["2001"]]),
    Dens2022 = viscount_fmt_number(p22 / ar, 1L),
    Sites = viscount_fmt_number(n_sites, 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  df_r
})
ext_df <- do.call(rbind, ext_rows)
rownames(ext_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  ext_df,
  "Supplementary provincial benchmarks (1933, 1962, 1982, 2001), 2022 density (persons per km²) and catalogued settlement counts.",
  c("Province", "1933", "1962", "1982", "2001", "2022 (per km²)", "Sites"),
  list(label = "tab:regions-extra", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

```{r tab-corpora, results='asis'}
corp_names <- c(
  INEC_Ecuador_Censos_1950_2022_and_pobecu = "INEC National Censuses (1950-2022) and 2024 Revision",
  INEC_Ecuador_ADM3_Parroquias_2024 = "INEC Administrative Division Parishes (2024)",
  INEC_Ecuador_Empadronamientos_1857_1962 = "Historical Empadronamientos and Pre-1962 Counts (1857-1962)"
)
corp_rows <- lapply(ledger_data$saturation_audit$exhausted_corpora, function(cp) {
  nm <- if (cp$name %in% names(corp_names)) unname(corp_names[[cp$name]]) else cp$name
  data.frame(
    Corpus = nm,
    Tier = "Primary national statistical archive",
    Rows_In_Bounds = viscount_fmt_number(cp$total_rows_in_bounds, 0L),
    Processed = viscount_fmt_number(cp$rows_processed, 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
corp_df <- do.call(rbind, corp_rows)
rownames(corp_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  corp_df,
  "Primary national statistical corpora processed across Ecuador, 1857 to 2024.",
  c("Statistical Corpus", "Source Tier", "Rows in Domain", "Rows Processed"),
  list(label = "tab:corpora-ecuador", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

```{r tab-hgis, results='asis'}
hgis_rows <- lapply(sum_data$hgis_regime_summary, function(hg) {
  src_lbl <- gsub("_", " ", hg$source)
  data.frame(
    Regime = as.character(hg$snapshot_regime),
    Source = src_lbl,
    Units = viscount_fmt_number(hg$units, 0L),
    Pop_Sum = viscount_fmt_pop(hg$population_sum),
    Area_Sum = viscount_fmt_number(hg$area_km2_sum, 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
hgis_df <- do.call(rbind, hgis_rows)
rownames(hgis_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  hgis_df,
  "Historical GIS administrative snapshot regimes across Ecuador, 1870 to 2025.",
  c("Snapshot Year", "Boundary Dataset", "Unit-Years", "Cumulative Population", "Cumulative Area (km²)"),
  list(label = "tab:hgis-ecuador", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```
